_meta.convencao_de_pagina: Pages = PDF numbering (1-148 for DOCKHB; 1-2 for K8SB). The Docker Handbook PDF has no printed page number; there is no conversion map.

fontes.DOCKHB: The Docker Handbook - Learn Docker for Beginners (Farhan Hasin Chowdhury, freeCodeCamp, 1 Feb 2021, 148 pp.)
fontes.K8SB: Learn Kubernetes Basics (kubernetes.io, tutorial index page, 2 pp.; last modification cited: 14 Jan 2026)
fontes.12FACTOR: UNUSABLE: the Twelve-Factor-App.pdf file contains 12 'Page not found' pages. It is not a source.

containerizacao-conceito.name: Containerization concept and the problem it solves
containerizacao-conceito.summary: Package the code with all its dependencies to run uniformly on any infrastructure; the book motivates it with native build dependencies and differences between operating systems.
rules: The idea: develop and run in an isolated environment (container) identical to the deployment one, package app + dependencies + configuration into a single file (image) and distribute it through a central server (registry) (DOCKHB p.9).
Author's motivation: the real dependency list includes a C/C++ and Python toolchain (node-gyp), which is hard on Windows/Mac and inconsistent across operating systems (DOCKHB p.7-8).
Docker is one implementation among others; Podman (Red Hat) is mentioned; Kaniko and rkt are mentioned as not yet direct replacements (DOCKHB p.10).
not_in_book: Kernel namespaces/cgroups details.
Runtime comparison (containerd, CRI-O, runc).

container-vs-vm.name: Container vs virtual machine
container-vs-vm.summary: A container virtualizes the host OS (via the container runtime) instead of having a guest OS; that is why it is lighter than a VM.
rules: VM: hypervisor + full guest OS, long communication chain and overhead (DOCKHB p.19-21).
Container: uses the host OS through the container runtime, keeping isolation (DOCKHB p.21-22).
The book's practical proof: uname -a on the host and inside an alpine container show the same kernel (DOCKHB p.22).
On Windows containers use the WSL2 kernel; on macOS the default back-end is a VM on top of HyperKit (DOCKHB p.22-23) [DATED].
not_in_book: Security isolation limits between containers and VMs.
Native Windows containers.
datado: HyperKit on macOS is the 2021 description; current Docker Desktop uses other back-ends.

imagens-camadas-registry.name: Image, container, registry and Docker architecture
imagens-camadas-registry.summary: Image = read-only multilayer template; container = running image with a temporary writable layer; a registry stores and distributes images.
rules: Images are multilayer, self-contained, read-only files; the OCI standard allows an image built with Docker to be used with another runtime such as Podman (DOCKHB p.23).
Running a container creates a temporary writable layer on top of the read-only layers (DOCKHB p.23).
Docker Hub is the default public registry; Quay (Red Hat) is another; you can have your own registry and there is a local cache (DOCKHB p.23-25).
Architecture: dockerd daemon, docker client and a REST API between them (DOCKHB p.25-26).
docker run: if the image is not local, the daemon pulls it from Docker Hub; afterwards it stays in the local cache (DOCKHB p.27-28).
not_in_book: Internal format of manifests/digests.
Retention policies in registries.

instalacao.name: Docker installation
instalacao.summary: Docker Desktop on Mac/Windows (WSL2 on Windows); on Linux, Engine and Compose are installed separately.
rules: Windows: install WSL2, then Docker Desktop (DOCKHB p.12-13).
Docker Desktop bundles Engine, Compose, Dashboard and Kubernetes; on Linux there is no bundle (DOCKHB p.14).
Verification: docker --version and docker-compose --version (DOCKHB p.12, 13, 15).
The author uses only the command line, no GUI (DOCKHB p.16).
not_in_book: Current installation steps (check the current documentation).
datado: 2021 instructions: docker-compose as a separate binary, Ubuntu 20.10/Fedora 33, 'stable' channel. Today Compose is a plugin (docker compose); Docker Desktop licensing has changed.

ciclo-de-vida-container.name: Container lifecycle and commands
ciclo-de-vida-container.summary: docker <object> <command> <options>; run = create + start; stop (SIGTERM then SIGKILL) vs kill; start vs restart; rm/prune; --rm.
rules: Syntax restructured since version 1.13: docker <object> <command> <options> (DOCKHB p.29).
container stop sends SIGTERM and, if it does not stop within a certain time, SIGKILL; container kill sends SIGKILL directly (DOCKHB p.37).
start starts a stopped/dead container, detached by default and keeping ports; restart tries to stop and start (DOCKHB p.37-39).
container run = container create + container start (DOCKHB p.40).
Stopped containers remain on the system; container rm removes; container prune removes all stopped ones (DOCKHB p.41-42).
--rm removes the container as soon as it stops; the author uses it in most examples (DOCKHB p.43-44).
container ls shows only running ones; --all includes those that already ran; the ID appears as 12 characters out of 64 (DOCKHB p.33-34).
--name sets a name; container rename works on a running or stopped container (DOCKHB p.34-36).
not_in_book: docker system prune, docker stats, docker top.
Restart policies (--restart).

portas-detached-interativo.name: Publishing a port, detached mode, interactive mode and exec
portas-detached-interativo.summary: Containers are isolated: you must publish host:container ports; -d runs in the background; -it for interactive images; exec runs a command in an active container.
rules: --publish <host port>:<container port>: requests to the host port are forwarded to the container port (DOCKHB p.30-31).
By default the container runs in the foreground; --detach/-d keeps it in the background and prints the ID (DOCKHB p.32).
In docker run the image must come last; whatever comes after it is an argument to the entry-point (DOCKHB p.32).
-it = -i (input) + -t (pseudo-tty); without -it an 'ubuntu' image shows nothing useful (DOCKHB p.45-46).
For a command in a NOT running container: docker container run <image> <command>; in a running one: docker container exec <container> <command>, with -it if interactive (DOCKHB p.48, 125-126).
not_in_book: Publishing on a specific IP (127.0.0.1:8080:80), UDP, -P.
docker attach.

bind-mounts-volumes.name: Bind mounts, anonymous volumes and named volumes
bind-mounts-volumes.summary: A bind mount links a host directory to a container directory in both directions; an anonymous volume protects a directory (e.g. node_modules); a named volume persists database data.
rules: Bind mount: bidirectional link between a local directory (absolute path) and a directory in the container; -v/--volume option with up to three fields, the third optional (DOCKHB p.51).
In dev, a bind mount of the source code triggers hot reload; but it covers the node_modules installed in the image and breaks the app (vite: not found) (DOCKHB p.92-95).
The book's solution: an anonymous volume for node_modules (-v /home/node/app/node_modules), managed by the daemon (DOCKHB p.95-96).
Databases (PostgreSQL) write to /var/lib/postgresql/data; without a volume, data is lost if the container is destroyed; use a named volume (volume create/ls) (DOCKHB p.113-115).
The author prefers a named volume over a bind mount for database data (DOCKHB p.115).
.dockerignore has no effect on bind mounts (DOCKHB p.102).
not_in_book: Volume backup/restore, volume drivers, UID/GID permissions on bind mounts, --mount, tmpfs.
volume prune.

dockerfile-basico.name: Dockerfile: instructions and build
dockerfile-basico.summary: Dockerfile = instructions; each instruction creates a layer; docker image build <context>; tag repo:tag; FROM, EXPOSE, RUN, CMD, COPY, ADD, ARG, WORKDIR, USER, ENV, ENTRYPOINT appear in examples.
rules: Every valid Dockerfile starts with FROM (DOCKHB p.55).
EXPOSE is documentation: --publish is still needed (DOCKHB p.55).
RUN and CMD can be shell form or exec form; the book uses exec form in CMD (DOCKHB p.55-56).
Running NGINX as a single process (daemon off) is considered good practice in containers (DOCKHB p.56).
Build: docker image build <context>; context = directory accessible to the daemon; the Dockerfile is looked up in it (DOCKHB p.56-57). --file for another name (DOCKHB p.91).
COPY <source> <destination>; ADD also downloads from a URL but does not extract; ARG declares variables used as ${name} (DOCKHB p.66, 68-69).
WORKDIR affects the following COPY, ADD, RUN and CMD; the default is the root (DOCKHB p.89).
ENTRYPOINT turns the image into an executable: docker run arguments go to the program (DOCKHB p.48, 52, 82).
Copy package.json and run npm install before copying the rest of the code (DOCKHB p.88-90) [inference by the package author: this favors layer caching; the book does not state the reason].
not_in_book: HEALTHCHECK, LABEL, VOLUME, SHELL, ONBUILD, STOPSIGNAL.
A rule to prefer COPY over ADD.
Ordering layers to maximize cache as an explicit rule.

tags-e-latest.name: Image tags and the latest tag
tags-e-latest.summary: The tag identifies a build/version; with no tag it becomes latest, which does not guarantee it is the latest version.
rules: Syntax --tag <repository>:<tag> (DOCKHB p.58-59); image tag to re-tag later (DOCKHB p.60).
Without a tag, the image gets latest; this does not mean the most recent version, and Docker does not check (DOCKHB p.86).
The name (repository) does not change after upload; the tag can change (DOCKHB p.85).
Tag examples: mysql:5.7, node:lts, node:lts-alpine (DOCKHB p.59, 86).
[extrapolation] Pinning the version in FROM is a recommended practice; the book's examples use ubuntu:latest/alpine:latest (DOCKHB p.55, 77), which p.86 itself implicitly discourages.
not_in_book: Digest pinning (@sha256).
Tagging strategy in CI (semver, commit sha).

otimizacao-de-imagens.name: Image optimization: layers, cleanup and Alpine
otimizacao-de-imagens.summary: Remove build packages in the same RUN instruction that installs them; switching the base to Alpine drastically reduces size in the book's experiment.
rules: image history lists the layers; each instruction records changes; there is one writable layer per container (DOCKHB p.62-63).
The union file system avoids duplicating data and allows earlier layers to be used as build cache (DOCKHB p.63-64).
Packages installed and removed in separate RUNs still add to the final size; do install+compile+remove in a single layer (DOCKHB p.75).
Clean the package cache in the same RUN: apt-get clean && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* (DOCKHB p.55-56, 74).
Result measured by the author: 343MB -> 81.6MB (optimized ubuntu) -> 12.8MB (alpine); official nginx:stable image 133MB (DOCKHB p.72, 76-77, 80).

Alpine (musl libc + busybox) is light (ubuntu ~28MB vs alpine 2.8MB, at the time) and is described by the author as secure and suited to containers; apk add --no-cache and --virtual .build-deps + apk del (DOCKHB p.77-78).
Package names change between distributions (DOCKHB p.79).
not_in_book: distroless/scratch, slim.
musl vs glibc compatibility risks.
docker build --squash, BuildKit cache mounts.
datado: Sizes and versions (ubuntu 28MB, nginx 1.19.2, libssl1.1, python2 in apk) are from 2021.

multi-stage.name: Multi-stage builds
multi-stage.summary: Build in one stage with the toolchain and copy only the artifacts to a lean final image.
rules: In production the app becomes static files (npm run build) and only needs a server such as nginx; the node image is large and unnecessary (DOCKHB p.96-97).
Pattern: FROM node:lts-alpine as builder ... ; FROM nginx:stable-alpine ; COPY --from=builder /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html (DOCKHB p.97-98).
In the example API, stage 1 installs python/make/g++ for node-gyp and npm install --only=prod; stage 2 copies node_modules and sets NODE_ENV=production and USER node (DOCKHB p.118-119).
The final image contains only what is needed and discards the rest (DOCKHB p.97, 101).
not_in_book: --target to stop at a stage.
Cache between stages in CI.

usuario-nao-root.name: Non-root USER and environment ENV
usuario-nao-root.summary: The book runs the app as the node user instead of root and mentions Docker/Node good practices, without going deep into security.
rules: By default Docker runs containers as root; the author notes this can be a risk and recommends a non-root user when possible (DOCKHB p.89).
The node image already ships the node user; USER node sets it as the default (DOCKHB p.89).
NODE_ENV=production is important for the example API (DOCKHB p.119).
not_in_book: Hardening (cap-drop, read-only, seccomp, AppArmor), vulnerability scanning, image signing, secrets management.

dockerignore.name: .dockerignore
dockerignore.summary: List of files excluded from the build; analogous to .gitignore.
rules: The file must be in the build context; listed entries are ignored by COPY (DOCKHB p.101-102).
Book example: .git, *Dockerfile*, *docker-compose*, node_modules (DOCKHB p.101-102).
It does not affect bind mounts (DOCKHB p.102).
not_in_book: Excluding .env/secrets from the context as a security practice (it is [extrapolation]).

redes.name: Docker networks: default bridge vs user-defined
redes.summary: For two containers to talk, use a user-defined bridge; on it automatic DNS resolves container names.
rules: Inside a container, 127.0.0.1 is the container itself: it does not reach the database in another container (DOCKHB p.103).
Using the container IP (container inspect) is not recommended: the IP may change when the container is recreated (DOCKHB p.103-104).
The book's answer: put the containers on a user-defined bridge network (DOCKHB p.104).
Drivers listed: bridge (default), host, none, overlay, macvlan; only bridge is used in the book (DOCKHB p.104-105).
User-defined bridge: automatic DNS by name, better isolation, connect/disconnect on the fly; the default bridge only allows IP (DOCKHB p.106-107).
Automatic DNS requires user-defined names (--name); random names do not work (DOCKHB p.110).
Commands: network create/ls/connect/disconnect/rm/prune; --network in run/create (DOCKHB p.107-111).
not_in_book: Internal networks, aliases, IPAM, custom DNS.
Overlay/macvlan details.
Networks in Compose beyond the example (p.141-144).

app-multicontainer-manual.name: Multi-container app without Compose (notes-api + PostgreSQL)
app-multicontainer-manual.summary: Network + named volume + database container + API image, with environment variables and shell scripts/Makefile to manage everything.
rules: postgres requires POSTGRES_PASSWORD; POSTGRES_DB names the database; --env passes variables (DOCKHB p.112).
The API receives DB_HOST (the database container's name), DB_DATABASE and DB_PASSWORD (DOCKHB p.123-124).
container logs <name>, with -f/--follow to follow (DOCKHB p.115-117).
container exec to run migrations on the running API (DOCKHB p.125-126).
Management through boot.sh/build.sh/destroy.sh/stop.sh + Makefile (DOCKHB p.127-128).
[inference] The password 'secret' in --env is from the didactic example; the book does not discuss secrets management.
not_in_book: Docker secrets, .env files, vaults.
Waiting for database readiness before the API.

compose-basico.name: Docker Compose: file and services
compose-basico.summary: Compose defines the multi-container app in YAML; each container is a service. The book uses file version 3.8 and the docker-compose binary.
rules: Compose is aimed at development and testing; using it in production is 'not recommended at all' according to the book (DOCKHB p.129).
Each container is a service; docker-compose.yaml file with version "3.8", services, volumes (DOCKHB p.130-132).
Each service needs a ready image (image) or build (context + dockerfile) (DOCKHB p.132-134).
container_name overrides the default <directory>_<service>; image has the same default; a named volume without name uses <directory>_<key> (DOCKHB p.133-135).

A service references another by service name (DB_HOST: db) (DOCKHB p.134); [observation] the text on p.134 says db will be replaced by the IP of the 'api' service, but the example shows it refers to the db service: an author slip.
Top-level volumes define the named volumes used by the services (DOCKHB p.132, 135).
not_in_book: depends_on, healthcheck, profiles, extends, env_file, secrets, deploy/resources, override files, Compose Specification.
datado: docker-compose (v1, Python) is discontinued; today it is 'docker compose' (v2 plugin). The 'version' field is obsolete in the current Compose Specification. The book's 3.8 is not the 'latest version' today.

compose-comandos.name: Compose commands
compose-comandos.summary: up/start/stop/down/ps/exec/logs, run in the directory of the YAML file.
rules: Every docker-compose command must be run in the folder of docker-compose.yaml (DOCKHB p.135).
up builds missing images, creates and starts containers; --detach/-d; --file/-f only if the name differs; --build forces a rebuild (DOCKHB p.135-137).
start only starts existing containers, it does not create them (DOCKHB p.137).
ps lists only the containers of the YAML (DOCKHB p.137).
exec <service> <command> does not need -it (DOCKHB p.138).
logs <service>, -f to follow; leaving the log does not stop the container (DOCKHB p.138-139).
down stops and removes containers and networks; --volumes removes named volumes; stop stops and keeps the containers (DOCKHB p.139-140).
not_in_book: docker compose logs of all services with timestamps, restart, pull, config, run, scale.

compose-fullstack-nginx.name: Full-stack with Compose: nginx as router and isolated networks
compose-fullstack-nginx.summary: Four services (db, api, client, nginx) on two bridge networks; nginx receives everything and routes /api to the backend.
rules: All requests reach nginx (router): if the endpoint has /api it goes to the backend; otherwise, to the frontend (DOCKHB p.141).
Reason: the frontend runs in the browser (served from the container), so the Compose network does not work for it to find the API; nginx, inside the container, reaches all services (DOCKHB p.141).
By default Compose creates one bridge and attaches everything; the author defined two networks (frontend and backend) for isolation; nginx sits on both (DOCKHB p.143-144).
restart: unless-stopped appears in the nginx service (DOCKHB p.143).
The nginx configuration is outside the book's scope (DOCKHB p.142).
not_in_book: TLS, load balancing, nginx health checks, detailed production configuration.

publicar-imagens.name: Publishing images to a registry (Docker Hub)
publicar-imagens.summary: Login, tag <user>/<image>:<tag> and docker image push.
rules: Free Docker Hub account: unlimited public repositories and one private (DOCKHB p.83) [DATED].
docker login asks for user and password and warns that the password is stored unencrypted, suggesting a credential helper (DOCKHB p.83-84).
To publish, tag in the format <user>/<image>:<tag> and docker image push (DOCKHB p.84-86).
not_in_book: Access tokens, authenticated private registries, signing, automatic scanning, CI.
datado: Free-account limits and the pull rate limit policy have changed since 2021.

kubernetes-k8sb.name: Kubernetes (only what K8SB and DOCKHB say)
kubernetes-k8sb.summary: K8SB is just the index page of the 'Learn Kubernetes Basics' tutorial: objectives and six modules. It does not teach objects or commands.
rules: Tutorial objectives: deploy a containerized application on a cluster, scale the deployment, update it with a new software version and debug (K8SB p.1).
Kubernetes is described as a production-ready open source platform, based on Google's experience in container orchestration (K8SB p.1).
It helps ensure that containerized applications run where and when you want and find the resources they need (K8SB p.1).
Modules: 1 Create a cluster, 2 Deploy an app, 3 Explore the app, 4 Expose it publicly, 5 Scale, 6 Update (K8SB p.2).
It points to the 'Learning environment' page and the 'Using Minikube to Create a Cluster' tutorial (K8SB p.2).
The Docker Handbook mentions Kubernetes only as part of Docker Desktop (DOCKHB p.14).
not_in_book: Pod, Deployment, Service, Node, namespace, kubectl, manifest YAML, Ingress, ConfigMap/Secret, probes, rolling update (module 6 is only listed), HPA, persistent volumes, Helm.
Any kubectl command (all use is [extrapolation]).

twelve-factor.name: Twelve-Factor App (source unavailable)
twelve-factor.summary: The Twelve-Factor-App.pdf in this folder has 12 'Page not found' pages. No content: the agent does not cite Twelve-Factor as a source.
rules: Any statement about 12-factor is [extrapolation] and must be flagged; re-obtain the source (12factor.net) and regenerate the package to promote items to [from source].

Docker Handbook points that merely resemble 12-factor, without citing it: configuration through environment variables (DOCKHB p.112, 123-124), a single foreground process (DOCKHB p.56) and logs via container logs (DOCKHB p.115-117). They are not from Twelve-Factor.
not_in_book: The 12 factors, their names and rationale.
